- **charsight** — See the text that is in your file but not on your screen: Unicode tag smuggling, zero-widths, variation-selector carriers, bidi overrides and homoglyphs decoded into the message they actually spell, plus invisible text in a PDF and hidden text in a web page, with a cleaned file out. The situation: you are about to paste a downloaded README, AGENTS.md or "skill" into an agent that will act on it, or the text you copied out of a chatbot just broke a CSV import, a diff or a build; the query is "remove invisible characters from chatgpt text" (also "zero width character detector", "what is this weird character in my code"). Audience: low millions of one-off uses a year, hundreds of thousands of distinct people — a whole crowd of commercial single-textarea sites (gptcleanuptools.com, cleangpt.app, gptcleanup.com) exists purely to do the easy tenth of this, which is direct evidence of the volume, and the second audience is every developer whose agent reads text they did not write. Tech: zero model, zero runtime network, instant on a phone — first-party detectors over code points, not regex over strings: Tags block U+E0000–U+E007F with the ASCII payload DECODED AND SHOWN, variation selectors U+FE00–FE0F and U+E0100–E01EF, zero-widths U+200B/200C/200D/FEFF/2060, bidi controls U+202A–202E and isolates U+2066–2069 with a first-party UAX#9 reordering pass rendering what a human sees beside what the parser sees, soft hyphen U+00AD, the space family (U+00A0, U+202F, U+2009, U+3000), private-use areas, and Unicode TR39 confusables.txt (745,683 B, 9,994 lines) plus intentional.txt (6,569 B) COMPILED AT BUILD TIME into a compact packed table so it works offline; mixed-script and TR39 restriction-level analysis catches `раypal` in a link or an identifier; `Intl.Segmenter` at grapheme granularity so a base character carrying twelve variation selectors renders as ONE badged cell; an OffscreenCanvas 64 px glyph-raster alpha diff that proves two code points are indistinguishable in the user's actual font stack rather than asserting it from a table; `TextDecoder` streaming for large files; `String.prototype.normalize` NFKC/NFKD fold-and-compare; optional token view via `gpt-tokenizer` 3.4.0 o200k_base LAZY-IMPORTED BY SUBPATH ONLY (the package is 53,103,516 B unpacked and the barrel import adds ~50 MB to the bundle). THIS ENTRY SUPERSEDES THE HIDDEN-TEXT CANDIDATE (hiddenink) AND ABSORBS ONLY ITS CHEAP SIGNALS: HTML/Markdown `display:none`, `visibility:hidden`, `font-size:0`, off-screen `clip-path`, `aria-hidden` and comments, plus PDF text render mode 3 and 7 read straight off `setTextRenderingMode` in `pdfjs-dist` 6.2.108 `getOperatorList()` and near-white fills read directly from `setFillRGBColor`/`setFillGray` — NO colour-space conversion, NO glyph bounding boxes, NO occlusion-behind-opaque-rect detection, and the UI says which signals are implemented; .docx/.xlsx/.pptx ARE EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE because docxray in this same queue owns Office files. Input: paste, drop files, or a folder; output: `cleaned.<ext>` byte-identical to the input except the code points your policy touched so it drops straight back into the repo or the CMS, `findings.csv` (file, line, column, byte offset, code point, Unicode name, block, category, decoded payload, action taken) and a single-file `report.html` quoting the smuggled message — the thing you attach when reporting a poisoned README. Privacy: nothing leaves the tab and there is no network request at runtime at all. Displaces nothing sold directly at consumer scale — enterprise DLP and Snyk Team at $25/dev/month bundle bidi detection as one rule, and the free field hands you text in a box rather than a file plus an evidence CSV. Ship `public/samples/poisoned-readme.md` (a Tags-block instruction payload, a bidi-override function name, a Cyrillic-а homoglyph inside a URL, 40 zero-widths and a legitimate emoji ZWJ sequence that must NOT be flagged). HONESTY GATE: it must never answer "did an AI write this" — narrow no-break spaces and curly quotes come from Word, keyboards and CMSes, and a probability here lands its false positives on non-native English writers; state that flatly in the UI. Hard part: highlighting must be driven through `Intl.Segmenter` with the mark applied inside the grapheme cluster or emoji ZWJ, Indic and Hangul text renders shredded and the tool looks broken on ordinary international text.

- **leakmap** — Drop your `.env` and your built `dist/` folder and find out, byte for byte, which of your secrets your app shipped to the public — plus the source code your sourcemaps are handing out for free. The situation: you vibe-coded an app, deployed it to Vercel/Netlify/Cloudflare Pages/GitHub Pages, and you are doing a pre-launch sanity pass (or you just got a provider abuse email); the query is "did i deploy my api key to vercel" (also "is it safe to put api key in vite env"). Audience: hundreds of thousands a year — everyone shipping AI-assisted frontends plus every junior on Copilot or Cursor; one-off per project rather than daily, but the number of such apps shipped weekly makes the converting slice comfortably six figures. Tech: no model, no network, entirely deterministic, and the precision comes from using YOUR OWN secrets as the needle — read `.env`/`.env.local`, extract the values, and run a first-party Aho-Corasick multi-pattern search over the streamed build bytes so one pass finds every occurrence with zero entropy heuristics and zero false positives, reporting file, byte offset and 60 characters of context; sourcemap forensics finds `.map` files and both `//# sourceMappingURL=` forms including inline `data:application/json;base64`, and a first-party base64-VLQ decoder over `mappings` maps each leaked literal's byte offset back to the exact original `file:line:column`, with `sourcesContent` unpacked by `fflate` 0.8.3 (796,742 B, zero deps) into a real directory tree; first-party rules for this exact failure mode — `dangerouslyAllowBrowser`, client-side calls to `api.openai.com`/`api.anthropic.com`/`generativelanguage.googleapis.com`, key shapes `sk-proj-`, `sk-ant-api03-`, `AIza…`, `hf_`, `xox…`, `sk_live_`, and `eyJ` JWTs base64url-decoded far enough to read the `role` claim so a Supabase `anon` key reports as fine and a `service_role` key as a five-alarm fire; input via `showDirectoryPicker` on Chromium desktop, `<input webkitdirectory>` elsewhere, or a dropped ZIP as the mobile path, scanned across a `navigator.hardwareConcurrency` Worker pool so a 40 MB `.next` output does not freeze the tab. PER THE JUDGES: REFUSE INDEX MAPS (`sections`) LOUDLY rather than half-decoding them, since a partially-correct decoder points at the wrong original line silently; THE .ENV VALUES LIVE IN MEMORY ONLY — never OPFS, never localStorage — AND ARE MASKED TO THEIR LAST FOUR CHARACTERS IN EVERY ARTEFACT INCLUDING `exposure-report.html`, stated on the input control itself; AND ALWAYS PRINT THE RAW GENERATED-FILE BYTE OFFSET BESIDE THE MAPPED SOURCE LOCATION so a bad mapping is visible rather than confidently wrong. Artefact: `exposure-report.html` (single self-contained file, each leaked value masked, with its shipped location and its original source line), `rotate-these.csv` (one row per credential: provider, where it leaked, the provider's own rotation URL), `recovered-source.zip` (your original tree rebuilt from `sourcesContent` — the proof that ends the argument about whether the exposure is theoretical), and `fix.md` with the literal config lines (`build.sourcemap: false`, `productionBrowserSourceMaps: false`, the webpack/Rollup/esbuild equivalents) plus the rename off `VITE_`/`NEXT_PUBLIC_`. Privacy: uploading your `.env` to a scanner to find out whether your `.env` leaked IS the disclosure — here the secrets never touch disk, never touch the network, and never appear unmasked in an output file. Displaces Snyk Team and Socket.dev at $25/dev/month and GitGuardian/Nightfall enterprise DLP, none of which the person shipping a weekend app buys; `grep` over a minified bundle finds nothing without knowing the value, and truffleHog/gitleaks scan git history and source, not build output, and need an install. Ship `public/samples/leaky-build.zip` (a real Vite `dist` with three planted keys, one inline base64 sourcemap, one external `.map` with `sourcesContent`, and a `service_role` JWT) beside `public/samples/env.sample`. Hard part: the VLQ decoder — build it against a fixture suite of real Vite, Next, webpack and esbuild output with known answers, because a half-right mapping points at the wrong source line with total confidence.

- **ghostdep** — Check that every package name your AI just told you to install actually exists — and that the one that does exist is not a six-day-old squat of the name it hallucinated — then leave with a pinned, hash-locked `requirements.txt` or `package.json`. The situation: an assistant handed you twenty-two import lines and you cannot tell a real package from a plausible one; the query is "does this npm package exist" (also "pip install package not found" and "is this package safe to install"). Audience: 300k–1M a year — the exposed population is everyone who has pasted AI-generated code with imports (most of 26M+ Copilot users plus Cursor and chat-assisted developers) and the converting slice is anyone who has been burned once or read a slopsquatting headline; deliberately NOT scoped to security professionals. Tech, all CORS re-verified with a third-party Origin: `registry.npmjs.org/{pkg}` returns ACAO `*` on 200 AND on 404 so existence is one cheap fetch; `registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/search?text=` (ACAO `*`) returns `downloads.weekly`, `downloads.monthly`, `dependents`, `date` and `links.repository` in one round trip; `api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/{pkg}` is ACAO `*`; the abbreviated packument (`Accept: application/vnd.npm.install-v1+json`) adds `hasInstallScript`, and the full packument gives `time.created` and `maintainers` for the age-and-solo-publisher signals; PyPI's `pypi.org/pypi/{pkg}/json` is ACAO `*` on 200 and 404 and the PEP 691 index `pypi.org/simple/{pkg}/` with `Accept: application/vnd.pypi.simple.v1+json` is ACAO `*` and carries every file's sha256, which is what makes the `--require-hashes` artefact real; HONEST GAP, verified: `pypistats.org` sends NO `access-control-allow-origin` at all, so PyPI download counts are unreachable from a tab and the UI SAYS SO rather than faking a number, falling back to first-upload date, release count, yanked status, repository-link presence and maintainer email domain. Typo detection is a BK-tree over Damerau-Levenshtein with keyboard-adjacency weighting against a build-time-generated top-5,000 npm + top-5,000 PyPI name table shipped as ~180 KB of packed strings so it works offline and instantly; Node builtins, `node:` specifiers, Python stdlib, relative paths and workspace names are excluded by first-party lists so they never alarm. PER THE FEASIBILITY FIX, SHIP THE BUNDLED ~400-ENTRY IMPORT-NAME MAP (`cv2`→opencv-python, `yaml`→PyYAML, `PIL`→Pillow) AND DEFER THE LIVE WHEEL-INTROSPECTION RESOLVER TO V2; PER THE AUDIENCE FIX, SCALE THE EDIT-DISTANCE THRESHOLD WITH NAME LENGTH AND WITH THE POPULAR NEIGHBOUR'S DOWNLOAD RATIO AND EXPOSE BOTH AS SLIDERS with the live match list underneath, or `ms`, `qs` and `ws` generate constant false alarms and the tool loses trust in its first minute; never assert an import-name mapping, show the evidence. Input is a pasted chat answer, a dropped file or a `requirements.txt`/`package.json`; output: those files rewritten with every verified package pinned to an exact version plus its hash (sha256 `--require-hashes` straight from PyPI's own index, sha512 `integrity` for npm), `unresolved.txt` holding every hallucination with its nearest neighbours attached, and `dependency-audit.csv` (name, exists, first published, weekly downloads, repo, nearest popular neighbour, edit distance, verdict); the headline is "of the 22 packages in this answer, 2 do not exist and 1 was created 6 days ago". Privacy, stated precisely: your code stays in the tab and is never sent; the only requests are anonymous GETs for the package NAMES you chose to check, which npm and PyPI necessarily see — and the tool never installs, never executes and never resolves a private registry. Displaces Socket.dev at $25/dev/month and Snyk Team at $25/dev/month, neither bought by a hobbyist or a student; `npm view` and `pip index` need the toolchain installed, answer one name at a time and know nothing about a name's age or the popular name it is one keystroke from. Ship `public/samples/ai-answer.md` (a chat reply with 22 imports including two names that do not exist, one six-day-old squat one character from a popular package, and `cv2`/`yaml`/`PIL`). Hard part: threshold calibration — the two sliders with the live match list, as above.

- **docxray** — See everything still hiding inside a .docx before you email it: every tracked change with its author and date, every comment thread including the resolved ones, hidden text, and the part of each photograph you cropped away but did not remove. The situation: you are on a Mac, or a Chromebook, or in Word on the web, about to send a contract, a report or a board pack outside your organisation — and Microsoft's Document Inspector does not exist for you at any price; the query is "check word document for tracked changes before sending" (also "does word for mac have document inspector", "how to see hidden comments in a docx"). Audience: order 5M English-speaking professionals email Office files externally (≈1.37M US lawyers, ≈1.6M accountants, ≈900k HR, plus procurement, grants and academia), the Mac/Chromebook/web-Office subset structurally locked out of Document Inspector is a large and growing fraction, and the frequency is per-send — hundreds of thousands acting per year. PER THE FEASIBILITY REVIEW THIS IS .DOCX-ONLY AND STRICTLY READ-ONLY: NO `cleaned.docx`, NO OPC REWRITE, NO .XLSX AND NO .PPTX IN V1 — emitting a rebuilt package means owning `[Content_Types].xml`, `_rels` and every part-level relationship, and one Word repair dialog ends the tool forever; it REVEALS and then tells you the exact Word menu path that removes each finding. Tech: `fflate` 0.8.3 (796,742 B, zero deps) over the OPC ZIP and `DOMParser` over the parts — `w:ins`/`w:del`/`w:moveFrom`/`w:moveTo` with `w:author`, `w:date` and the literal text of each change; `word/comments.xml` plus `commentsExtended.xml` for threaded replies and resolved state; `w:vanish` hidden text and white-on-white runs; footnotes, endnotes, headers, footers, `w:docVars` and `docProps/custom.xml`; the full distinct-author list from `settings.xml` rsids and the change records; embedded `oleObject`/`package` relationships; and the finding that exists in no product at any price — DrawingML `a:srcRect` l/t/r/b crop fractions compared against the real pixels in `word/media/*`, each image decoded with `createImageBitmap` and re-rendered FULL-FRAME on a canvas with the visible rectangle outlined, so you see the 3.2× of photograph you were about to send. Zero model, zero network, works offline on a locked-down school Chromebook and on mobile Safari. Artefact: `disclosure-report.html` — self-contained and printable, every finding with its literal content and every uncropped image inline, suitable as a pre-send checklist or an incident record; `findings.csv`; and `revealed-images/` containing each cropped photograph exported as a full-frame PNG with the visible rectangle boxed. The headline: "this file exposes 34 tracked changes by 3 authors, 11 comments, hidden white text, and 4 photographs containing 3.2× more image than is visible." Privacy: the file is parsed in the tab and never uploaded — which matters because the document you most need to check is the one you are least allowed to upload. Displaces Litera's Metadact/Clean line at $195–$1,000+/user/year as a Windows-and-Outlook DMS add-in; Document Inspector is free but Windows-only, absent from Word for Mac and Word on the web, and removes without ever showing you what it is removing — so even Windows users get something it refuses to give. Ship `public/samples/contract-draft.docx` (34 tracked changes by 3 authors, 11 comments including 2 resolved threads, a `w:vanish` paragraph, white-on-white text, and 4 photos cropped to a third of their pixels). Hard part: joining runs and changes correctly through nested tables, textboxes and content controls — unit-test the traversal against a fixture set produced by Windows Word, Mac Word, Google Docs export, LibreOffice and Pages, and report "this file records no tracked changes" as a distinct, confident state rather than an empty list.

- **unfence** — The missing bridge between a chat window and your project folder: pack the folder into one paste-ready bundle, then paste the answer back and get a real diff, a `git apply`-clean patch and the files written to disk. The situation: the model returned six files, you are on a locked-down work laptop where you cannot install Node, and you are about to hand-create them one by one; the query is "copy code from chatgpt to files" (also "how to give chatgpt my whole codebase", "apply chatgpt code changes to project"). Audience: hundreds of thousands and plausibly more — everyone using chat rather than an agent CLI, which is the large majority of AI-assisted coders, including the non-professional builders and non-Python creatives; repomix, code2prompt, gitingest and uithub are widely used for the OUTBOUND half alone and every one of them needs Node or a public repo URL and not one does the inbound half, which is the whole opportunity. It is also the highest-frequency tool in this queue: used on every multi-file answer, not once a project. Tech outbound: `showDirectoryPicker` on Chromium desktop, `<input webkitdirectory>` as the universal fallback, dropped ZIP as the mobile path; A DELIBERATELY DOCUMENTED .GITIGNORE SUBSET (literal paths, extensions, directory names, leading-slash anchoring) WITH THE HONOURED RULES PRINTED IN THE UI — per the feasibility fix, full gitignore semantics (negation re-inclusion under an ignored directory, trailing-slash directory rules, mid-path `**`) is a fixture-suite project of its own and almost nobody implements it correctly; a hard refusal list (`.env*`, `id_rsa`, `*.pem`, `.git/objects`) overridable only by typed confirmation, which is what stops this becoming a leak tool; null-byte binary sniffing; a budget slider counted in real tokens with `gpt-tokenizer` 3.4.0 o200k_base IMPORTED BY SUBPATH, NEVER THE BARREL (the package is 53 MB unpacked), with per-file toggles sorted by cost. Inbound is the unbuilt half and is entirely first-party: a fenced-block parser recovering each block's intended path from four competing conventions (info-string ``ts title="src/app.ts"``, a first-line `// src/app.ts` comment, a preceding bold or heading line, `=== src/app.ts ===` separators), collapsing regenerated duplicates of the same path keeping the last, detecting elision markers (`// ... rest unchanged`, `# ...`) and REFUSING to write an elided file over a real one, and detecting truncation by unclosed fences and unbalanced braces. DROP THE THREE-WAY MERGE ENTIRELY per the feasibility fix: diff the model's block against the on-disk file only with `diff` 9.0.0 (615,597 B, zero deps), present per-hunk accept/reject, and rely on an automatic pre-write `backup-<timestamp>.zip` as the safety net instead of conflict detection. PATH INFERENCE MUST BE VISIBLE AND CORRECTABLE, NEVER SILENT: every block shows its inferred path with the evidence that produced it in an editable field, anything below the confidence bar lands in a manual bucket, and nothing is written without a dry-run listing plus the backup ZIP. Output writes back through the same `FileSystemDirectoryHandle`, or downloads a ZIP where the handle is unavailable; `fflate` 0.8.3 both directions; everything heavy in a Worker. Artefact: `bundle.md` (tree header plus per-file fences, sized to your budget), `changes.patch` (a genuine unified diff with correct `a/`/`b/` prefixes and hunk headers that `git apply` accepts), `updated.zip` and/or files written straight into your folder with `backup-<timestamp>.zip` beside them, and `skipped.md` listing every block the model returned elided or truncated so nothing is half-applied. Privacy: your source never leaves the tab and there is no network request at all — which is the point on a machine where you are not allowed to install a packer or paste your repo into a website. Displaces a $20/month Cursor or Copilot subscription — i.e. you pay to stop copying and pasting — and it is for the people who are not going to do that, on machines where they cannot. Ship `public/samples/small-app.zip` and `public/samples/model-reply.md` (six fenced blocks across all four path conventions, one regenerated duplicate, one elided file, one truncated file). Hard part: path inference — the visible-evidence editable field, the manual bucket and the dry-run above; and note it never scans a build output, which is leakmap's job.

- **crowdsize** — Before you email that spreadsheet of people to someone, find out how many rows identify exactly one person — then generalise, suppress, and leave with an anonymised CSV and a risk report you can staple to an ethics or DPIA submission. LEAD WITH THE ORDINARY DOOR AND PUT THE THEORY BEHIND IT, per the audience fix: the tool opens on "how many rows in this spreadsheet identify one person?" with the quasi-identifier set AUTO-PROPOSED and the unique rows shown AS REAL RECORDS before the words k-anonymity, l-diversity or t-closeness appear anywhere. The situation: you are about to send a participant list, a patient extract or an FOI response to a collaborator and you do not know whether the postcode-plus-birth-year-plus-sex combination gives someone away; the query is "how to anonymise a csv before sharing". Audience, stated honestly: the converting core is professional — US health researchers, registry and QI staff, clinical-trial coordinators, public-health analysts, IRB submitters, DPOs and academic social scientists, order 300k–800k in the US and over 1M worldwide under GDPR pseudonymisation duties, of which perhaps a tenth act in a given year; the much wider front door (councils, schools, charities, HR analysts, FOI responders, data journalists) converts less well because that person cannot pick a quasi-identifier set unaided, which is exactly why the set is auto-proposed and every change re-scores live. Tech: SHIP CSV/TSV ONLY IN V1 — cut Parquet (hyparquet) and .xlsx per the feasibility fix, since the whole value is in the engine and the person emailing a spreadsheet of people has a CSV or can export one. First-party streaming parser over `File.stream()` → `TextDecoderStream` (RFC-4180 quoting, BOM handling, delimiter sniffing) across a `navigator.hardwareConcurrency` Worker pool; a column profiler doing type inference plus a HIPAA Safe Harbor 18-identifier matcher combining a header-name lexicon with value-shape tests (MRN, SSN structure, phone, email, URL, IP, VIN, full dates, ages >89, ZIP) and UK/EU equivalents (NHS number mod-11, NI number, full postcode); a ~4 KB shipped static asset holding the public list of 3-digit ZIP prefixes with population ≤20,000 that Safe Harbor requires be recoded to 000. The engine is one pass — hash each row's quasi-identifier tuple into a `Map<string,count>` in a Worker — yielding the k-distribution, singleton count and per-row k for 1M rows × 8 columns in seconds; l-diversity is a nested count and t-closeness is Earth-mover distance over a one-dimensional distribution. The generalisation ladder re-scores live: date→month→year, age→5- or 10-year bands with 90+ aggregation, ZIP→ZIP3 with the restricted list applied, rare-category collapse to Other, top/bottom coding, and record suppression at your k threshold, with a utility readout (% cells generalised, % rows suppressed, per-column entropy retained) and a Canvas 2D k-histogram. Zero model, zero network, no WASM, no CORS surface. Artefact: `anonymised.csv`; `risk-report.html` — self-contained, stating the exact quasi-identifier set, k threshold, ladder applied and the before/after k-distribution in the shape an IRB, DPIA or ROPA reviewer expects, WITH THE LIMITATION PRINTED INSIDE THE REPORT ITSELF (k-anonymity resists linkage, not homogeneity or background-knowledge attacks) so the artefact carries its own caveat to whoever receives it; and `suppressed-rows.csv` so you know what you lost. The headline: "47 of your 12,480 rows are unique on {postcode district, birth year, sex} — those 47 people are re-identifiable by anyone holding an electoral roll." Privacy: the file that must not be emailed is also the file that must not be uploaded to a checker — it is parsed and rewritten entirely in the tab, offline. Displaces ARX, which is free and excellent but is a Java desktop download requiring a JRE and therefore unavailable on an NHS laptop, a Chromebook, a locked SOE or a phone, and Amnesia likewise; the commercial tier (Privitar, Tonic.ai, Aircloak-style platforms) is contact-sales. There is no browser option at any price and the cost of getting it wrong is a documented $125,000 penalty. Ship `public/samples/participants.csv` (12,480 synthetic rows with exactly 47 singletons on postcode district + birth year + sex, plus a sensitive diagnosis column for the l-diversity view). Hard part: choosing the quasi-identifier set is the whole failure mode in either direction — auto-propose it from the identifier matcher, show the singleton records as real rows the moment the file loads, and make every add/remove re-run the single pass so the consequence is visible rather than theoretical.

- **veracite** — Check every quotation and citation in a draft against the PDFs you actually have on disk — which quotes exist verbatim, which are near-misses with the edits shown, which cite the wrong page, and which appear nowhere at all. REFRAME AWAY FROM THE COURTROOM, per the audience fix: the landing page is the researcher with a folder of PDFs or a Zotero export, NOT the sanctioned lawyer — that lawyer has a Westlaw seat, not the case PDFs — and the page states plainly that case-law citations are out of scope in v1 because no CORS-open case-law API exists. The situation: you let an assistant draft over sources you already hold, and you need to know which quoted sentences are actually in them before your supervisor, your editor or a reviewer finds out; the query is "check if a quote is real in a pdf" (also "verify ai citations against sources"). Audience: ~4M US graduate students and faculty who write with sources, plus journalists, policy analysts, consultants and medical writers — low hundreds of thousands acting per year, per-draft frequency. Tech: `pdfjs-dist` 6.2.108 `getTextContent()` using each item's `transform`, `width` and `hasEOL` to rebuild reading order across columns and repair hyphenation across line breaks; `mammoth` 1.12.0 (2,166,337 B) for .docx sources; `fflate` 0.8.3 + `DOMParser` for .epub; first-party .txt/.md/.html. Each source is normalised (NFKC, lowercase, quotes and dashes unified, whitespace collapsed) into one character stream with a monotonic offset map back to (file, page, character). THE PER-SOURCE PREFLIGHT IS NON-NEGOTIABLE AND IS ADOPTED WHOLESALE FROM THE RIVAL CANDIDATE: report "text layer: yes/no, N characters extracted" for every file before matching and mark any source with no text layer UNSEARCHABLE so its quotes are never reported NOT FOUND — the difference between a result and an accusation. Matching is a first-party rolling-hash k-gram inverted index (k=32 normalised characters) built across a Worker pool, candidates confirmed with banded Smith-Waterman and `fastest-levenshtein` 1.0.16 (21,281 B) so a quote with one changed word is NEAR MATCH with the diff shown rather than absent; quote extraction handles straight, curly, guillemet and CJK pairs, blockquote paragraphs and any ≥12-word run marked as quoted; pinpoint checking parses "p. 14", "at 1207" and "¶ 32" and compares them to the page the match landed on. Citation layer: first-party extraction of DOIs (`10.\d{4,9}/\S+`), PMIDs, ISBNs and arXiv ids, then optional resolution — VERIFIED CORS-OPEN with a third-party Origin: `api.crossref.org` (ACAO `*`), `api.openalex.org` (`*`), `api.datacite.org` (echoes Origin), `eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov` esummary (`*`), `api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1` (`*`); VERIFIED CLOSED: `export.arxiv.org` returns 200 with NO ACAO header at all, so arXiv ids are routed through OpenAlex via their `10.48550/arXiv.*` DOIs — the resolver fuzzy-compares resolved title, first author and year against what the draft claims, which catches the real-DOI-wrong-paper hallucination; a HARD OFFLINE SWITCH disables all resolution in one click. CUT THE 31 MB SEMANTIC PARAPHRASE TIER AND THE OPFS INDEX FROM V1 — the whole ethical premise is that a paraphrase is not a quotation, so a semantic layer is the one feature that can only blur the product's central distinction. Artefact: `quote-audit.csv` (one row per quotation with source file, page, character offset, match type, edit distance, cited pinpoint vs actual) plus `draft-annotated.html` with every quotation linked to its exact source location and the NOT FOUNDs in red. The headline: "7 of your 41 quotations do not appear in any source you gave me." Privacy: the unpublished draft and the confidential sources are exactly the two things you cannot hand to a vendor; with the offline switch on there is not one network request. Displaces CiteCheck AI and Counsel Stack subscriptions, Scite at $20/mo, and Westlaw/Lexis cite-checking bundled into four-figure annual seats — none of which can see the PDFs on your disk, which is where the quote actually has to be; the realistic alternative is a research assistant at $40–$150/hour. Ship `public/samples/draft-with-quotes.md` and `public/samples/sources.zip` (six open-access PDFs, one deliberately image-only so UNSEARCHABLE is demonstrated on first run; 41 quotations of which 7 are planted fabrications and 5 are near-misses). Hard part: pdf.js text fidelity — mitigate with the character-count preflight and a bundled planted-quotation self-test that runs on first load, because a NOT FOUND is only believable if the tool has just proved it can find things.

- **regraft** — Put the generation recipe back into an AI image that a platform stripped — and take it out of the copy you are about to post. LEAD WITH RESTORE, NOT STRIP, per the duplication review: the strip half is a commodity that shipped `metascrub` already covers in a different container and three commercial sites sell, so recovery is the headline, stripping is a secondary tab, AND THE WORD "METADATA" MUST NOT APPEAR IN THE HEADLINE. The situation: Discord, Reddit or a re-encode flattened the workflow out of your ComfyUI image and you can no longer drag it back into ComfyUI, or you are about to post an image whose embedded prompt names a client; the query is "comfyui workflow missing from png" (also "discord removed my png metadata", "get prompt back from stripped image"). Audience: hundreds of thousands to low millions — it reaches past the hobbyist to anyone who posts an AI image from any generator, hosted or local; r/StableDiffusion is 984k members and the hosted-generator population is far larger, the frequency is per-post rather than once-ever, and a commercial micro-industry (aimetadatacleaner.com, removeailabel.com, Gumroad strippers) already takes money for half of what this does. Tech: a first-party PNG chunk-list rewriter — because every chunk carries its own CRC32 and IDAT is untouched, both stripping and re-injecting are byte-exact rebuilds with zero re-encode and zero quality loss (verified on real ComfyUI files: every metadata byte sits before IDAT, at offsets 33 and 1,742 with IDAT at 17,872, so a 60 MB PNG parses instantly on a phone); `png-chunks-extract` 1.0.0, `png-chunks-encode` 1.0.0 and `png-chunk-text` 1.0.0 as the reference implementation with a first-party streaming writer for large files; `DecompressionStream`/`CompressionStream('deflate')` for the zTXt dialect; `exifr` 7.1.3 (1,291,466 B, zero deps) for the A1111 JPEG/WebP EXIF `UserComment` dialect. Dialects read, written and re-injected: A1111 `parameters`, ComfyUI `prompt` + `workflow`, InvokeAI `invokeai_metadata`, NovelAI `Comment`+`Software`. PER THE FEASIBILITY FIX, SHIP PNG AND WebP ONLY IN V1 — the ISO-BMFF `moov/udta/©cmt` and EBML `Tags` video walkers and the ComfyUI API-graph→UI-graph reconstructor (laying out a missing `workflow` from a surviving `prompt` block by topological rank) are the stretch, not the day-one build. Input: drop an image (and optionally a sidecar); output: `restored.png` — your stripped image with its sidecar re-injected so it drags into ComfyUI again, which is the hero and which nobody sells at any price — plus `workflow.json`, `prompt.json` and `parameters.txt` sidecars extracted from an intact file, and `clean.png` with the exact byte delta shown. Privacy: an embedded prompt routinely contains client names, personal detail and unreleased concepts; the file is rewritten in the tab, the pixel bytes are copied rather than re-encoded so the strip is provably lossless, and nothing is uploaded — unlike every hosted stripper, whose business model requires you to hand it the file you were worried about. Displaces aimetadatacleaner.com and removeailabel.com, which sell the strip half as a hosted upload, and a Gumroad category of paid stripper downloads. Ship `public/samples/flux-example.png` (real ComfyUI `prompt` 1,887 B + `workflow` 10,329 B chunks), `public/samples/flux-example-stripped.png` and its extracted sidecar, so the whole round trip is demonstrable offline. THE PRODUCT'S SPINE IS THE AFTER-SCAN GREEN GATE: re-parse the written file with a fresh parser and print the residual byte count per chunk type, because reporting "clean" while leaving NovelAI's `Comment`+`Software`, an `invokeai_metadata` chunk, an XMP `iTXt`, an `eXIf` chunk or a C2PA JUMBF box is the single failure that ends the tool's credibility. HONESTY GATE: it reports exactly what a file declares about its own origin and nothing more — it cannot tell you whether an image was AI-generated, and the absence of a chunk proves nothing, because platforms strip these on upload.

- **peelback** — Recover the earlier versions still buried inside a PDF (every incremental save is physically present in the file) and read the production chain that is always there even when there are none. MAKE THE ALWAYS-PRESENT EVIDENCE THE HEADLINE so no session ends empty, per the audience fix: the `/Producer`, `/Creator`, `/CreationDate`, `/ModDate` chain, the XMP `xmpMM:History` array with each save's `softwareAgent`, embedded-image metadata, and any `/Sig ByteRange` showing bytes appended AFTER a digital signature — "this statement's Producer is a browser print-to-PDF, which is not what a bank sends" is a usable finding on a single-revision file; revision recovery is the jackpot path, not the promise. The situation: an applicant's payslip, an invoice or a bank statement looks very slightly off and you have no way to check it; the query is "how to tell if a pdf payslip has been edited" (also "check if a bank statement is fake"). Audience: roughly 10–11M individual US landlords screening applicants, plus small-business accounts-payable staff, HR verifying offer letters, insurers, and mortgage and auto-loan processors at institutions too small for Inscribe or Ocrolus — hundreds of thousands a year, with the honest caveat printed on the page that Save As flattens history so most files will yield one revision, which is precisely why the producer chain leads. Tech: a first-party byte-level PDF structure parser, which is the point — pdf.js deliberately hides this layer and every free viewer stops at `/Producer`. Scan the ArrayBuffer for every `%%EOF`, validate each candidate by parsing the preceding `startxref` and confirming the xref parses (so an `%%EOF` inside a stream cannot create a phantom revision), then follow the `/Prev` chain through BOTH classic xref tables and PDF 1.5+ cross-reference streams — the latter requires `DecompressionStream('deflate')` on the `/Type/XRef` stream plus first-party PNG-predictor unfiltering (Up/Paeth, `/DecodeParms /Predictor 12 /Columns n`) before the entry table is readable; detect `/Linearized` in the first object so a linearised file's early `%%EOF` is not misreported as history. Each recovered revision is materialised by slicing bytes `[0, eof_i]` — itself a complete, valid, standalone PDF — AND GATED TWICE: never list a revision unless its xref parses AND the truncated byte range renders in `pdfjs-dist` 6.2.108 without error. `exifr` 7.1.3 (1,291,466 B) reads embedded-image metadata. PER THE FEASIBILITY FIX, THE 150 DPI PIXEL-DIFF WITH CONNECTED-COMPONENT CHANGE BOXING IS V2 — v1 ships revision extraction plus the per-revision producer/XMP/signature evidence, which is the strongest artefact anyway and needs no rendering beyond the validity gate. Artefact: `revision-1.pdf` … `revision-N.pdf`, each a complete standalone PDF you can open, print and attach to a dispute — the earlier version of the document IS the evidence — plus `changes.csv` (revision, producer, creator, timestamps, signature status) and a self-contained `report.html`. Privacy: a disputed payslip or tenancy application carries someone's salary, address and employer; it is parsed in the tab and never uploaded, which also means no third party holds a record that you ran a fraud check on a named person. Displaces Inscribe, Resistant AI and Ocrolus — enterprise document-fraud platforms sold contact-sales to lenders, not landlords — and a forensic document examiner at roughly $200–$500/hour; Acrobat Pro at $19.99/mo will not show you prior incremental saves either, because Save As silently flattens them away. Ship `public/samples/statement-edited.pdf` (three incremental saves with a changed figure on page 2) and `public/samples/signed-then-appended.pdf` (a `/Sig ByteRange` with bytes added after signing). HONESTY GATE: it reports what the bytes contain and never a verdict — absence of revisions proves nothing about authenticity, and a phantom "earlier version" inside a fraud accusation is the one unrecoverable failure, which is why the parse-and-render gate is mandatory. Hard part: xref-stream decoding and predictor unfiltering — build a fixture suite of real PDFs from Word, Acrobat, LaTeX, Chrome print-to-PDF and a scanner, with known revision counts.

- **cuepoint** — Type what you are looking for and find the exact moment in a long video file — "red car turning left", "someone at the front door" — then cut those moments out as clips, without the footage ever leaving your machine. LEAD THE LANDING PAGE ON THE TWO NAMED JOBS, per the audience fix — "find the crash in your dashcam footage" and "find the delivery in a week of doorbell clips" — with general video search second. The situation: you have three hours of loop-recorded dashcam video and an insurer wants the ten seconds around the impact; the query is "find moment in dashcam footage" (also "search video for something without uploading"). Audience: tens of millions of consumer dashcams ship annually and the home-security population (Ring, Nest, Reolink, Eufy) is in the tens of millions with smart search sold as a subscription; honest converting reach is hundreds of thousands a year, plus teachers and students with lecture recordings and editors logging raw footage. Tech: decode with `mediabunny` 1.52.2 `Input` + `VideoSampleSink` over WebCodecs `VideoDecoder`, hardware-accelerated, the path already proven in the catalogue by vidwell and gifsmith so there is no ffmpeg.wasm COOP/COEP exposure — AND SAMPLE KEYFRAMES RATHER THAN DECODING EVERY FRAME DOWN TO 1 fps, per the feasibility fix: dashcam and doorbell GOPs are typically 1–2 s so keyframe-only sampling lands near the target rate for free and removes the decode bottleneck, which is the cost the design otherwise underweights. Preprocess with `createImageBitmap(frame, {resizeWidth: 256, resizeQuality: 'low'})` + OffscreenCanvas in a Worker pool bounded to `navigator.hardwareConcurrency` — mandatory, because transformers.js's JS-side image preprocessing measures 8.6–35.2 ms/image, 1.4–7× the inference cost. Embed with `Xenova/mobileclip_s0` `vision_model_quantized.onnx` = 11,846,843 B (or `vision_model_fp16.onnx` = 22,876,479 B on WebGPU), measured 6.3 ms/image inference and 67.2 images/sec end-to-end on WebGPU versus 4.9/sec on single-threaded WASM — quote both tiers with a wall-clock ETA before starting; query with `text_model_quantized.onnx` = 42,799,238 B + `tokenizer.json` = 2,224,081 B (56,870,162 B total), measured 8 ms per query, and it REQUIRES `padding:'max_length', max_length:77` or transformers.js throws "Non-zero status code returned while running Add node". THE TWO TOWERS RUN IN SEPARATE DEDICATED WORKERS WITH SEPARATE ORT ENVIRONMENTS — several onnxruntime-web WebGPU sessions in one context reproducibly corrupt each other. Scoring is first-party brute-force cosine over one `Float32Array` (a 2-hour video at 1 fps is 7,200 × 512 f32 = 14.7 MB, sub-10 ms, so re-query is live on every keystroke), then a temporal median filter and non-maximum suppression collapse per-frame scores into moments — WITH THE MEDIAN WINDOW, NMS MERGE GAP AND MINIMUM DURATION EXPOSED AS VISIBLE CONTROLS, not magic constants — and RANK, NEVER THRESHOLD, BY DEFAULT: MobileCLIP scores are uncalibrated, 0.24 is an excellent match for one query and noise for another, so show the top N with thumbnails immediately and let the user drag the cut-off while watching real frames. Clip export via mediabunny's `Conversion` with trim, cutting on keyframes where possible; explicit `VideoFrame`/`ImageBitmap` `.close()`, a resumable OPFS checkpoint and a stated file ceiling keep a 4 GB phone alive. Artefact: `clip_001.mp4` … the actual extracted moments as playable keyframe-aligned files you hand to an insurer or a solicitor; `cuepoints.csv` (query, start, end, peak score, peak timestamp); `chapters.vtt`, which YouTube, Plex, VLC and Jellyfin read natively so your queries become permanent chapter marks on the file; and `index.f32` + `index.json` so the video stays searchable forever without re-embedding. DROP THE CONTACT-SHEET PNG — shipped sentrywell already emits one and the overlap is gratuitous; sentrywell finds movement by frame differencing and cannot tell a person from a curtain, which is the product difference. Privacy: dashcam and doorbell footage shows your street, your neighbours and other people's children, and a 6 GB file never leaves the machine. Displaces Ring Protect Plus and Nest Aware monthly subscriptions for smart search over your own footage, muse.ai hosting-plus-search, and Mixpeek's metered multimodal API; VLC can only search subtitles. Ship `public/samples/dashcam-clip.mp4` (8 minutes with one near-miss, one red car turning left and one pedestrian crossing) with three prefilled queries. Hard part: uncalibrated similarity — the rank-with-live-thumbnails interaction above is the entire answer, and it must be the default rather than a setting.

- **unflatten** — Turn any flat photo into a 3D parallax clip that moves — depth estimated on your own GPU, exported as a ready-to-post MP4 — with the 16-bit depth map and a retroactive portrait-mode blur thrown in. The situation: you have a scanned photograph of a grandparent, or a downloaded image with no captured depth data that your phone's own portrait trick cannot touch, and you want the LeiaPix effect without a credit meter; the query is "make a photo 3d parallax video free" (also "depth map from image for controlnet"). Audience: hundreds of thousands to low millions per year — Immersity AI (ex-LeiaPix) sustains $4.99/mo for 500 credits ≈ 25 3D images plus a $14.99 Pro tier on this single effect, which is clean market proof, and Facebook 3D Photos and MyHeritage Deep Nostalgia both went viral at tens of millions; a second audience wants only the depth map, since the ComfyUI/A1111 population (123,151 and 164,338 GitHub stars, r/StableDiffusion 984k) generates ControlNet depth inputs constantly and currently installs a Python node to do it. Tech: `onnx-community/depth-anything-v2-small` `onnx/model_q4f16.onnx` = 19,126,267 B on WebGPU (measured 491 ms per 640×480 image on an Apple Metal-3 adapter — the lightest first-run download in this queue and comfortable on a 4 GB phone), falling back to `model_quantized.onnx` (int8) = 27,258,801 B on WASM; verified 302→206 with ACAO `*` and Range support; driven through `@huggingface/transformers` 4.2.0's depth-estimation pipeline in a dedicated Worker. Rendering is first-party WebGL2: an adaptive 256×256 triangulated grid vertex-displaced by the depth texture, with camera paths (dolly, orbit, sway, Ken Burns-with-depth) evaluated per frame; encoding with `mediabunny` 1.52.2 driving WebCodecs `VideoEncoder` to H.264 MP4 at 1080×1920 / 1080×1080 / 1920×1080, 30 fps — the same path already proven by shipped wavewell and vidwell, which is why ffmpeg.wasm and its COOP/COEP trap never enter the picture. A first-party 16-bit greyscale PNG writer (~80 lines) is genuinely required because Canvas 2D only does 8-bit and 8-bit depth banding is visible in ControlNet; the same depth field drives a graded circle-of-confusion background blur in a fragment shader with a draggable focal plane. PER THE FEASIBILITY FIX, SHIP V1 AS A SINGLE DISPLACED-GRID MESH WITH THE CAMERA EXCURSION AUTO-CAPPED to the range where disocclusion is not visible — layered thresholding with per-layer alpha dilation and push-pull pyramid inpainting is V2 — AND NORMALISE PARALLAX AMPLITUDE PER IMAGE, since depth-anything emits relative inverse depth with no metric scale and portraits and landscapes otherwise behave wildly differently; expose the depth-discontinuity threshold with a live hole-map overlay so the user can see exactly what is being invented. Artefact: `parallax.mp4` (H.264, no watermark, portrait/square/landscape, loops seamlessly), `depth.png` (true 16-bit greyscale, correctly scaled, immediately usable as a ControlNet depth input), `bokeh.jpg` (a physically graded depth-of-field blur with an adjustable focal plane — portrait mode applied retroactively to a photo that never had it), and an optional red/cyan anaglyph PNG. Privacy: the photographs people most want to animate are of dead relatives, and there is no way to un-upload one — this never uploads and works offline after the 19 MB model caches. Displaces Immersity AI at $4.99/mo for ~25 images and $14.99/mo Image Pro with a watermarked 720p free tier, no commercial use and monthly credit expiry; CapCut and Photoshop's Depth Blur require subscriptions and, in CapCut's case, an upload. Ship `public/samples/portrait.jpg` and `public/samples/landscape.jpg` (CC0, one with strong foreground/background separation and one without) so per-image amplitude normalisation is visible on first run. Hard part: disocclusion — the smeared halo around a foreground subject is where every cheap implementation dies, so the auto-capped excursion plus the live hole-map overlay are what make a single-sheet v1 honest rather than obviously broken.

- **tomecast** — Turn a PDF, EPUB or DOCX into a real MP3 audiobook with chapter marks and a studio-quality voice, generated entirely on your own device. The situation: you have a 300-page report, a set of course readings or an unpublished manuscript and a commute, and every converter you find caps you at five pages or wants $139 a year; the query is "convert pdf to audiobook free" (also "text to speech long pdf mp3"). Audience: the largest honest one in this queue — text-to-speech is a standard accommodation for dyslexia at roughly 10% population prevalence, plus students with course readings, commuters, indie authors auditioning manuscripts and anyone with a long PDF; high hundreds of thousands a year for a free, unmetered tool, against Speechify marketing to tens of millions. Tech: `kokoro-js` 1.2.1 driving `onnx-community/Kokoro-82M-v1.0-ONNX` `model_q8f16.onnx` = 86,033,585 B (verified 302→206, ACAO `*`, Range-readable) plus exactly ONE voice pack per session at 522,240 B lazily fetched. ENGLISH ONLY, AND SAY SO PLAINLY — DROP THE ja/zh VOICES FROM THE PICKER ENTIRELY per the feasibility review: kokoro-js depends on npm `phonemizer` (eSpeak NG), while Kokoro's Japanese and Mandarin voices require `misaki[ja]`/`misaki[zh]`, which are Python, so those voices would mispronounce; this is an English audiobook tool, not a nine-language one. CUT THE kitten-tts WASM FALLBACK (it adds a first-party numpy `.npz` reader for a tier nobody should use), AND CUT PER-CHAPTER MP3s, `playlist.m3u` AND `chapters.cue` — one MP3 with real chapter frames is the artefact and the rest is packaging. MEASURE RTF ON THE FIRST 30 SECONDS AND PRINT THE WALL-CLOCK ETA BEFORE A SINGLE BYTE OF THE 86 MB MODEL DOWNLOADS: measured WebGPU fp32 is RTF 0.269 (~3.7× faster than real time, so a 4-hour book is ~68 minutes) while WASM q8 measured RTF 7.17 — SEVEN TIMES SLOWER THAN REAL TIME, i.e. 28 hours for the same book — so the WASM tier is refused with the number on screen rather than silently started. Input parsing: `pdfjs-dist` 6.2.108 text layer with per-item `transform` for column and heading inference and REPEATED-POSITION CLUSTERING to strip running headers and footers; `fflate` 0.8.3 + `DOMParser` for EPUB (OPF spine → chapter order); `mammoth` 1.12.0 for DOCX. Output: `mediabunny` 1.52.2 + `@mediabunny/mp3-encoder` 1.52.2 with a FIRST-PARTY ID3v2.4 WRITER emitting CTOC + CHAP chapter frames alongside TIT2/TPE1/TALB and cover art taken from the PDF's first page or the EPUB cover, so the file opens with a real chapter list in Apple Podcasts, Overcast, VLC and a car stereo; OPFS holds per-chunk PCM so a killed tab resumes instead of losing two hours; joins are made at zero crossings with equal-power crossfades or every sentence boundary clicks. Artefact: `audiobook.mp3` — one file, chaptered, tagged, ready to AirDrop to a phone, drop into a podcast app or put on a USB stick for the car — plus `chapters.txt` with timecodes. Privacy: the documents people most want read aloud are medical letters, legal bundles, unpublished manuscripts and licensed course readings; nothing is uploaded, and after the first run it works on a plane. The browser's own `SpeechSynthesis` API cannot substitute — it often routes to cloud voices and it cannot hand you a file. Displaces Speechify Premium at $139/yr or $29/mo billed monthly, Speechify Audiobooks $9.99/mo and Studio $19–49/user/mo, ElevenLabs from $5/mo metered by character, and NaturalReader and Murf per seat; the free web converters are metered hard (FreeTTS one PDF a day at five pages, ScreenApp three conversions a month). Ship `public/samples/short-book.epub` (a 6-chapter public-domain text, ~90 minutes of audio) and `public/samples/paper.pdf` (a two-column paper with running headers and dense reference markers). Hard part — and it makes or breaks the product, not the synthesis: THE TEXT-NORMALISATION PASS MUST BE A VISIBLE, EDITABLE PREVIEW OF THE LITERAL STRING THE MODEL WILL SPEAK, with header/footer clustering, hyphenation repair and citation/figure-marker suppression as toggles, because a 300-page PDF that reads "[14]" and "Fig. 3.2b" aloud every paragraph is unlistenable.
